newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Relief seen for SAfrica reserves in 97 -Old Mutual.
newsitem.headline: Relief seen for SAfrica reserves in 97 -Old Mutual.

text.p: South Africa should be able to rebuild its precarious foreign exchange reserves in 1997 after sharp falls last year, Old Mutual chief economist Dave Mohr said on Tuesday.
"The big positive is that during the course of 1996, we did not have capital outflows...we still had a net capital inflow," Mohr told an economic presentation.

"If we run a current account situation that's more or less balanced, let's say a small deficit, and we have the capital flows that we had last year, with all the uncertainty and trauma, we will have rebuilt our foreign exchange reserves."

South Africa's December total gold and foreign exchange reserves stood at 10.31 billion rand ($2.3 billion) from 10.93 billion rand the month before, which was not enough to cover even five weeks of imports.
Rising imports, falling commodity prices and smaller capital inflows kept foreign exchange reserves under increasing pressure last year, making the rand a target for speculative attacks.
On the balance of payments, Mohr anticipated further narrowing of the current account deficit after an improvement of about six billion rand -- at annualised rates -- in the third quarter of 1996.
But lower import tariffs and continued weak commodity prices could hamper improvement in the current account, he added.
Turning to the March 12 budget presentation, Mohr said a bold move on the government's part would be a further reduction in company taxes and some relief in direct income tax.
"Certainly, in terms of the middle income groups, this would be seen as a bold move because the tax curve is unbelievably steep these days," he said.
-- Vera von Lieres, Johannesburg newsroom 27 11 482 1003 ($ = 4.567 South African Rand)
